IFR—was thereby tainted and perhaps rendered an outright sham. Kristin 
E. Hickman and Mark Thomson, in their study Open Minds and Harmless 
Errors: Judicial Review of Postpromulgation Notice and Comment, 101 
Co r n e l l  L. Re v . 261 (2016), explain the argument this way: “Once an 
agency has publicly staked out a position and given effect to that position 
[by imposing an IFR],” it is possible that “forces like regulatory inertia, 
status quo bias, confirmation bias, and commitment bias all make it less 
likely the agency will deviate from its position.” Further, “citizens might 
not take seriously the opportunity to offer comments after a rule is in effect, 
believing that, because an agency has already committed to enforcing a 
particular rule, submitting comments would just be a waste of time.” If 
notice and comment risks becoming a sham in this way, then presumably 
courts should do something. Perhaps, if a court finds an agency lacked good 
cause to skip notice and comment on a certain IFR, the court should 
therefore invalidate the eventual final rule.
On the other hand, one can make the opposite argument: that an 
actual notice-and-comment process on the final rule renders it procedurally 
valid, regardless of whether an IFR was in place during that process and 
regardless of whether the IFR was itself validly excepted from notice and 
comment or not. If the IFR indeed lacked good cause, that would be reason 
to hold the IFR invalid (e.g., vitiating any enforcement adjudications that 
were completed while the agency was relying on the IFR) but not to hold 
the later final rule invalid.
If both these extremes seem unpalatable, another possibility would be 
to stake out a middle ground. As Hickman and Thomson note, some circuits 
did this by the 2010s, holding that the final rule was vahd only if the prior 
imposition of the IFR had not prevented the agency from keeping an “open 
mind” in shaping the final rule in response to comments.
In the following case, the Supreme Court reviewed a circuit decision 
that relied upon the “open mind” approach. The high court decisively 
rejected that approach and adopted the view that prior imposition of an 
IFR (regardless of whether the agency really had “good cause” to impose 
the IFR before notice and comment) had no effect on the validity of a final 
rule that did go through notice and comment.
